editorNote: Extra Edition: IBM's new 80286-powered PC/AT resets the performance and expansion baseline for the personal-computer market.
morningLine: The AT sets a new pace, software owns the showroom, and home computers find fresh routes onto the telephone line.

lead.headline: IBM's PC/AT Pushes Personal Computing Into a New Generation
lead.dek: The 80286-powered 5170 brings a 16-bit expansion path, a 1.2MB floppy, larger storage, and prices beginning at $3,995.
body: IBM's Personal Computer AT dominates the conversation as the week opens. Announced August 14, the machine type 5170 is built around Intel's 80286, with a 16-bit data path and 24-bit addressing. IBM says it performs more than twice as fast as current members of the PC family, a claim that marks a clean break from the original 8088 generation.

The $3,995 Model 68 supplies 256KB of memory and a 1.2MB 5.25-inch diskette drive. The $5,795 Model 99 raises memory to 512KB, adds a 20MB fixed disk, and includes a serial-and-parallel adapter. Neither price includes a display, keeping the AT firmly in the professional and office class even as its architecture points the way for future compatibles.

Eight expansion slots sit inside the new chassis, and six can accept either new 16-bit cards or familiar 8-bit PC boards. Conventional memory can reach 640KB, expansion memory as much as 3MB, and a socket is ready for Intel's 80287 mathematics coprocessor. IBM is selling speed without abandoning the card collections customers already own.

DOS 3.0 arrives as the operating-system partner, supporting the 20MB disk and the high-density floppy while retaining access to older disk formats. IBM also promises PC/IX 1.1 later in 1984 and XENIX support early next year, a signal that the AT is expected to serve more than ordinary single-user DOS work.

The announcement also brings the Enhanced Graphics Adapter and PC Network components into view. Taken together, the faster processor, broader bus, storage, graphics, and networking plans give software houses and clone makers a new target—and make the AT the week's unavoidable computing landmark.

stories.headline: Software Becomes the Home-Computer Show's Main Event
body: The Summer Consumer Electronics Show looks markedly different from last year's hardware rush. COMPUTE! calls 1984 the year of software: several machines once presented as contenders have disappeared or been withdrawn, but programs for the surviving installed bases continue to multiply.

The magazine names the Atari 1400XL, Mattel Aquarius line, Spectravideo machines, TI-99/4A, and Timex/Sinclair 1000 among casualties of the shakeout. Yet computer hardware and software still occupied more than 170,000 square feet at McCormick West, 25 percent more floor space than a year earlier.

The result is a market less dazzled by another new plastic case and more attentive to what owners can actually do. Commodore, Atari, Apple, IBM, VIC-20, and TI users all find fresh reviews, utilities, and type-in programs in the August shelves.

stories.headline: Low-Cost Adapters Put Atari and Apple Owners on the Line
body: Telecomputing is becoming an ordinary home-computer application. Advanced Interface Devices' R-Verter links the Atari serial bus to standard RS-232 modems, giving 400, 600XL, 800, and 800XL owners a direct route to telephone-line communications.

Apple users have two new approaches. ZOOM Telephonics' Networker bundles modem hardware and communications software for the II family, while Source Telecomputing's Apple Sourcelink is designed to help subscribers use The Source online service.

Even the orphaned Timex/Sinclair community is learning the ritual: an August user-group article walks members through modems and CompuServe. The growing lesson is clear—getting online is shifting from a specialist's project to a packaged purchase.

stories.headline: Infocom Sends Adventurers Diving for Treasure in Cutthroats
body: Infocom's latest text adventure casts the player as a diver on Hardscrabble Island, surrounded by sailors and competing plans to recover treasure from the sea. Released August 9, Cutthroats branches toward two different wreck expeditions.

Michael Berlyn and Jerry Wolper designed the nautical mystery with Infocom's portable Z-machine. Its package turns paper into part of the puzzle, supplying a tide table and shipwreck material among the physical clues that players must consult.
The release is a reminder that the software-led market has room for games that sell prose, inference, and imagination rather than arcade reflex alone.

curiosity.headline: IBM's New Powerhouse Comes With a Two-Hour Guided Tour
curiosity.summary: The PC/AT includes a self-booting tutorial disk called Exploring the IBM Personal Computer AT.
curiosity.detail: IBM estimates the tutorial takes 1.5 to 2.5 hours and supplies monochrome and color versions covering the keyboard, printer, storage, DOS, and text editing—an elaborate welcome mat for a professional machine.

milestone.title: IBM introduces the PC/AT
milestone.note: The 80286-based AT and its 16-bit expansion architecture reset the performance and hardware baseline for the IBM-compatible market.
